title: Ankara Restricts Black Sea Straits, Greenlights $280M Arms Sale to Ukraine, Fidan Warns of Russian Nuclear Risk
subhead: Turkey briefly halted then resumed Dardanelles transits for Black Sea-bound vessels after Fidan called for a Russia-Ukraine moratorium on attacking commercial shipping, while a US-notified $280M arms transfer from Turkish stocks to Kyiv — including 70 ATACMS missiles — signals a decisive strategic choice. Meanwhile, Fidan warned that Russia could resort to nuclear weapons if the war becomes existential, and a Ukrainian drone crashed in NATO-member Bulgaria one kilometer from a gas pipeline.

sections.heading: Turkey Restricts Then Resumes Black Sea Transits, Calls for Shipping Moratorium
sections.body:
Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan called on Saturday for a mutual moratorium on attacks against commercial vessels in the Black Sea, warning that the conflict has 'spread across the entire Black Sea' and that ships under the Turkish flag were also being hit. 'At first, they targeted ports and warships. Now they are attacking all merchant ships without distinction,' Fidan told Anadolu Agency, as reported by The Guardian and Le Temps.

Following Fidan's remarks, Turkey's Directorate General of Coastal Safety began restricting commercial vessel transits through the Dardanelles Strait for ships bound to the Russian port of Novorossiysk, Bloomberg reported. Some vessels were informed that transit permits were being withheld or delayed. Turkish officials subsequently stated that passage was continuing 'smoothly' but confirmed heightened security screening, Reuters/Economic Times reported. The initial restrictions appeared to be a brief but unprecedented use of Turkey's authority over the straits since the 1936 Montreux Convention.

The moratorium call follows an escalation in maritime attacks. In July alone, Ukraine recorded 35 Russian attacks on ships in port, 22 attacks on vessels at sea, and 67 strikes on port infrastructure, according to Kyiv Post. Ukrainian drone strikes also damaged commercial sites in Novorossiysk over the weekend, the city's mayor confirmed.
sections.whyItMatters: Turkey's brief restriction of strait transits is its most direct intervention in Black Sea shipping since the war began. It signals that indiscriminate attacks on commercial vessels — including Turkish-flagged ones — have crossed a threshold where Ankara is willing to use its Montreux Convention leverage to pressure both Moscow and Kyiv.

sections.heading: Turkey Clears $280M Arms Sale to Ukraine Including 70 ATACMS
sections.body:
The US State Department has notified Congress of a proposed $280 million arms transfer from Turkish stocks to Ukraine, according to documents published in the Congressional Record on August 6. The package includes 12 M270 MLRS launchers, 70 M39 ATACMS ballistic missiles, 2,524 M26 unguided rockets with DPICM cluster warheads, and 47,000 M509A1 203-mm cluster artillery shells, United24Media and Defense Express reported.

The M39 ATACMS variant has a range of approximately 165 kilometers and carries 950 M74 submunitions. The 12 M270 launchers reportedly represent the remainder of Turkey's M270 inventory, meaning Turkey is effectively divesting its entire tracked MLRS fleet. The transfer would involve Turkish defense companies MKE, ASFAT, and ARCA Savunma, alongside Bulgarian firm VTIC International and US contractors.

Congress has 15 calendar days to review the notification. Unless lawmakers adopt a joint resolution blocking it, the transfer can proceed. For Turkey, the sale would reduce stocks of aging systems while freeing resources for modernization, Defense Express noted.
sections.whyItMatters: This is not just an arms sale — it is a strategic decision to divest Turkey's entire M270 fleet to Ukraine. It deepens Turkey's military commitment to Kyiv at a moment when Ankara is also calling for a Black Sea shipping moratorium, positioning Turkey simultaneously as a mediator and an active military supplier to one side.

sections.heading: Fidan Warns Russia Could Use Nuclear Weapons If War Becomes Existential
sections.body:
In the same Anadolu Agency interview, Fidan warned that Russia could resort to nuclear weapons if the Ukraine war becomes an existential threat to the Russian state. 'When the war of attrition at the front turns into attrition in the rear, the question is no longer whether you lose the war or not, but whether you continue to exist as a nation. You use the last means you have,' Fidan said, as reported by United24Media and Anadolu.

Fidan said the issue had come up during his meetings with Russian officials and Western partners. 'During my visit to Russia, it seemed that this issue could be raised, as there was talk that the public was demanding something like this. We spoke about it with our Western partners, and they know this as well. This is a dangerous situation,' he added.

The warning comes as Zelenskyy reported that North Korea is now preparing to deploy up to 50,000 soldiers to Russia — up from the 30,000 estimated in July — and that a North Korean missile unit with 120 ballistic missiles and six launchers is deploying to western Russia, according to The Guardian.
sections.whyItMatters: Fidan's nuclear warning is unusually explicit for a NATO foreign minister — it acknowledges publicly what many officials discuss only privately. Combined with the ATACMS sale to Ukraine, it paints a picture of a Turkey that is simultaneously arming Kyiv, warning about nuclear escalation, and positioning itself as the mediator who understands both sides.

sections.heading: Ukrainian Drone Crashes in NATO-Member Bulgaria Near Gas Pipeline
sections.body:
A Ukrainian 'Maiia' decoy drone crossed from Romania into Bulgarian airspace on Saturday and exploded in a sunflower field approximately one kilometer from a compressor station for the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline that connects Turkey to Ukraine, Kyiv Post reported. Bulgaria's Defense Ministry identified the drone type as one widely used by the Ukrainian military and said there was no evidence the crash was intentional.

Bulgarian Foreign Minister Velislava Petrova summoned the Ukrainian ambassador for a meeting on Monday. Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev announced that Bulgaria would redeploy border guard personnel and anti-drone equipment from its border with Turkey to the Romanian border. Ukraine's Foreign Ministry said it was 'in close contact with Bulgarian authorities' and that its forces 'did not intentionally direct any assets toward Bulgaria,' The Guardian reported.

The incident follows a pattern of war-related drone incursions into NATO territory, but the proximity to a major gas pipeline that transits Turkish gas adds a direct Turkish interest to the episode.
sections.whyItMatters: A Ukrainian drone landing near a gas pipeline in a NATO state is a war-spillover incident that involves Turkey twice — once because the pipeline carries Turkish-bound gas, and again because Bulgaria is shifting security resources away from the Turkish border to the Romanian border, potentially creating a gap in NATO's southeastern flank.

sections.heading: PKK Criticises Peace Bill as Insufficient
sections.body:
The PKK on Sunday publicly criticised Turkey's proposed peace and disarmament bill that cleared the parliamentary Justice Committee last week with 360 votes. The group called the legislation insufficient for addressing the fate of its fighters, arguing that it focuses on disarmament and reintegration without guaranteeing broader political rights, MSN reported.

The 12-article bill establishes deferral of sentences — five years for sentences under 15 years, 10 years for longer ones — with permanent closure if no new offenses occur. It excludes those convicted of intentional murder and those sentenced to aggravated life imprisonment before June 1, 2005. Oversight would involve a council chaired by the vice president and a 17-member parliamentary monitoring committee. Justice Minister Akın Gürlek denied reports that former HDP co-chair Selahattin Demirtaş would be excluded, MSN and Kurdistan24 reported.

The PKK's criticism was predictable — no armed group accepts the first offer — but it sets the baseline for the negotiation ahead. The bill now moves to the general assembly.
sections.whyItMatters: The PKK's rejection sets the negotiation terms: the government must decide whether to amend the bill to draw the group toward disarmament or push it through as-is and risk the process stalling before it starts.

sections.heading: Mecca Pact Draws Israeli Condemnation and Regional Realignments
sections.body:
Israeli Diaspora Affairs Minister Amichai Chikli described the Mecca pact as 'a very dangerous and very troubling development' for Israel's security, arguing that Saudi Arabia's decision to align with Turkey — which Chikli said is engaged in a 'direct confrontation with Israel' — marks a significant shift. He called for Israel to deepen strategic partnerships with Greece, Cyprus, the UAE, and Somaliland, Greek City Times reported.

Iran responded with sharp hostility, with officials dismissing the pact as a 'paper agreement' and Tehran Times running an editorial calling it a 'sealed watermelon' — sweet only if opened, rotten if left sealed. India's external affairs ministry said it was 'closely following the development' but did not issue formal condemnation, with Firstpost analysis noting New Delhi's concern about Turkish military technology flowing to Pakistan.

Houthi forces attacked Saudi Aramco's Jazan refinery with a drone on Sunday, barely 48 hours after the pact signing. The Saudi Energy Ministry confirmed a fire was extinguished with no casualties. Neither Turkey nor Pakistan issued a response invoking the pact's mutual defense clause.
sections.whyItMatters: The Houthi strike on the Jazan refinery within 48 hours of signing was the first real test of the Mecca pact's mutual defense clause — and the silence from Ankara and Islamabad suggests the answer is consultation first, action later, if ever. Meanwhile, Israel's pivot toward Greece and Cyprus creates a parallel Eastern Mediterranean security architecture that directly counters Turkey's.

sections.heading: Iran Says Hormuz Deal With Oman in Final Stages
sections.body:
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday that an agreement with Oman on defining new shipping lanes through the Strait of Hormuz is in its 'final stages,' but reiterated that the strait would only reopen once the United States meets other conditions. Iran and the US are not engaged in direct talks, Araghchi said, but messages are being exchanged via intermediaries, The New Arab and Mehr news agency reported.

The Strait of Hormuz, which carried roughly a fifth of global oil and LNG shipments before Iran's blockade, remains closed. Reuters reported Friday that an agreement was close, but Araghchi's comments suggest Iran is holding the waterway as leverage for broader concessions from Washington.

For Turkey, any Hormuz reopening would ease global oil prices — directly affecting domestic inflation — but would also reduce the transit premium Turkey has been collecting on alternative energy routes through its territory.
sections.whyItMatters: A Hormuz deal would be the single biggest energy-market event in months, and Turkey is positioned on both sides of the equation: lower oil prices help inflation, but a reopened Hormuz reduces the strategic premium on Turkish transit routes. The longer Iran holds out, the more Turkey benefits from alternative corridor demand — and the more it risks if the strait suddenly reopens.

bottomLine: Turkey made its most direct intervention in the Black Sea shipping crisis yet, briefly restricting Dardanelles transits and calling for a moratorium on attacks against commercial vessels. The same weekend, a $280M arms package — including 70 ATACMS missiles and Turkey's entire M270 fleet — surfaced in US congressional notifications, confirming that Ankara is deepening its military commitment to Kyiv even as it positions itself as a mediator. Fidan's public warning about Russian nuclear escalation was the most explicit such statement from a NATO foreign minister. The Mecca pact's first 72 hours exposed its central tension: a Houthi drone hit a Saudi refinery and no one invoked mutual defense. And Iran's Hormuz negotiations inch toward completion, which could reshape Turkey's energy calculus overnight. The pattern is consistent — Turkey is stretching in every direction at once, and each bet is backed by a different set of assumptions about what the others will tolerate.
sources: The Guardian, Kyiv Post, Bloomberg, Reuters/Economic Times, United24Media, Anadolu Agency, New Arab, AP News, Firstpost, Tehran Times, Greek City Times, MSN, Defense Express, Congressional Record (govinfo.gov), Le Temps
